records.name: 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline
records.what: Free, confidential support for anyone who is thinking about suicide, in emotional distress, or in any crisis, 24 hours a day, every day of the year.
records.who: Anyone in the United States.
records.start: Call or text 988, or use the chat on the Lifeline website. In immediate danger, call 911.
records.note: In Washington State, dial 988 and choose option 4 for the Native and Strong Lifeline, answered by Native crisis counselors.

more.label: Native and Strong Lifeline fact sheet (Washington State)

records.name: StrongHearts Native Helpline
records.what: A helpline for Native Americans and Alaska Natives hurt by domestic or sexual violence. Advocates answer 24 hours a day, and the helpline describes itself as safe, confidential and anonymous.
records.who: Native Americans and Alaska Natives.
records.start: Call or text 1-844-762-8483, or open the chat on the website. The website has a quick exit: press the Esc key.
records.phone_note: 1-844-7NATIVE. Call or text, 24 hours a day

records.name: National Human Trafficking Hotline
records.what: Human trafficking means being made to work or to sell sex through force, lies or threats. This hotline connects people who are in that situation, or who got out of it, with support and services to get help and stay safe. It is confidential and open 24 hours a day. The hotline says it is not law enforcement and not an immigration agency.
records.who: Anyone, including a friend or relative who is worried about someone.
records.start: Call 1-888-373-7888, text 233733, or chat from the website. Deaf or hard of hearing: dial 711. Interpreters are available on phone calls. In immediate danger, call 911.

records.name: Missing and Murdered Unit (Bureau of Indian Affairs)
records.what: The Bureau of Indian Affairs unit that works on missing, murdered and human trafficking cases involving American Indians and Alaska Natives, together with tribal, federal, state and local police. It also coordinates victim services with families.
records.who: Anyone with information about a case, and families of missing or murdered Native people.
records.start: In an emergency call 911. To give a tip or ask the unit for help, call 833-560-2065 (Monday to Friday, 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m.), email OJS_MMU@bia.gov, or text BIAMMU and your tip to 847411.
records.phone_note: Monday to Friday, 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m.
records.url_label: About the Missing and Murdered Unit

records.name: National Domestic Violence Hotline
records.what: Live advocates answer by phone, text and online chat 24 hours a day, every day of the year.
records.who: Anyone.
records.start: Call 1-800-799-7233, text START to 88788, or use the chat on the website. In immediate danger, call 911.

records.name: National Sexual Assault Hotline
records.what: The national phone line for people who have been sexually assaulted, as listed by the federal Administration for Children and Families.
records.who: Anyone.
records.start: Call 1-800-656-4673. Native callers can also reach StrongHearts at 1-844-762-8483.

records.name: Crisis Text Line
records.what: Free, confidential crisis support by text message, 24 hours a day, from anywhere in the United States.
records.who: Anyone.
records.start: Text HOME to 741741. For Spanish, text HOLA to 741741. You can also chat from the website.

records.name: National Runaway Safeline
records.what: Free, confidential support for teens and young people who have left home or are thinking about it, 24 hours a day. USA.gov says it can arrange free transportation home or to other safe, stable housing.
records.who: Teens and youth, and adults who are worried about one.

records.name: Indian Health Service, tribal and urban Indian clinics
records.what: The Indian Health Service (IHS), tribal health programs and urban Indian programs give health care to American Indians and Alaska Natives. The IHS says it is not health insurance, and not an entitlement like Medicare or Medicaid.
records.who: The most common rule is enrollment in a federally recognized tribe. The exact policy is in the Indian Health Manual, so ask the clinic. Some tribally run clinics see only their own members.
records.start: Find the nearest clinic with the IHS Find Health Care tool, which lists IHS, tribal and urban clinics, and call ahead to confirm it offers what you need. To register, go to the clinic's patient registration office with proof of tribal enrollment.

more.label: IHS questions and answers for patients

records.name: Urban Indian health programs
records.what: Nonprofit health programs in cities, governed by boards that are at least 51 percent American Indian or Alaska Native. The IHS funds 41 of them, with more than 80 sites in 22 states. Services can include primary care, traditional healing, mental health and substance use counseling, and youth, elder and job programs.
records.who: Native people living in the city the program serves. Ask the program how it decides who it can see.
records.start: Find a program on the IHS map of Urban Indian Organizations, then call it.

records.name: Purchased/Referred Care: when the IHS pays for care somewhere else
records.what: Care at an IHS or tribal clinic is called direct care. Purchased/Referred Care (PRC) covers medical or dental care away from those clinics. The IHS says PRC is not an entitlement, and a referral does not mean the bill will be paid.
records.who: You must meet rules on tribal affiliation, where you live, giving notice, medical priority and other coverage you could use. PRC generally needs you to live on or near a reservation. It lasts 180 days after you move away; after that only direct care continues.
records.start: Before you get care outside the clinic, ask the clinic's PRC office what it needs from you and by when.

records.name: Health insurance rules for Native people (Marketplace, Medicaid, CHIP)
records.what: Members of federally recognized tribes and Alaska Native (ANCSA) shareholders can sign up for a Marketplace health plan in any month and change plans up to once a month. With income between 100% and 300% of the federal poverty level they can get a plan with zero cost sharing, and they pay nothing for care from Indian health providers at any income. In Medicaid and CHIP, people eligible for IHS services pay no premiums and no out-of-pocket costs for care from IHS, tribal or urban Indian programs. You can keep using those clinics after you enroll.
records.who: Marketplace rules: members of federally recognized tribes and ANCSA shareholders. Medicaid and CHIP rules: people eligible for IHS services; Medicaid's definition is broader and includes descendants.
records.start: Apply at HealthCare.gov or call 1-800-318-2596, open 24 hours a day except holidays. Answer yes when asked whether anyone is American Indian or Alaska Native. Have a tribal enrollment card, a BIA certificate of Indian blood or other proof of tribal affiliation ready.
records.url_label: HealthCare.gov: American Indians and Alaska Natives

more.label: Medicaid and CHIP for American Indians and Alaska Natives

records.name: SAMHSA National Helpline
records.what: Free, confidential information and referrals to treatment for mental health or substance use, in English and Spanish, 24 hours a day.
records.who: Anyone, including family members.
records.start: Call 1-800-662-4357 and say what kind of help you are looking for and where you live.

records.name: Wellbriety circles (White Bison)
records.what: White Bison is a Native American-operated nonprofit behind the Wellbriety Movement: sobriety, recovery and wellness grounded in Native culture. It keeps a list of Wellbriety circles, which are recovery and talking circles that meet in person and on Zoom.
records.who: Each circle says whether it is open to new people. Many are.
records.start: Open the circle list, find one near you or one on Zoom, and contact the facilitator listed for that circle.

records.name: Youth Regional Treatment Centers (IHS)
records.what: Residential treatment centers for Native youth who need help with alcohol or drug use, including youth who also have a mental health condition. The Indian Health Service runs some and tribes run others, in Alaska, Arizona, California, Nevada, New Mexico, North Carolina, South Dakota, Washington and other states.
records.who: American Indian and Alaska Native youth. Each center says who it takes; several list ages 12 to 17.
records.start: Open the IHS list, choose a center, and call it to ask how admission works and whether a bed is open.
records.url_label: IHS list of youth treatment centers

records.name: National Indian Child Welfare Association (NICWA)
records.what: Guides and support for Native families dealing with a child welfare case: the Indian Child Welfare Act, kinship care, tracing Native ancestry and finding low-cost legal help. NICWA says it cannot give legal advice or manage individual cases.
records.who: Parents, relatives and caregivers of Native children, and people who work with them.
records.start: Read the family resources first. If you still have questions, call (503) 222-4044 or email info@nicwa.org.

records.name: The Indian Child Welfare Act (ICWA): your family's rights
records.what: ICWA is a federal law for state court cases about foster care, adoption or ending parental rights when the child is a tribal member, or is eligible for membership and has a parent who is a member. The state must make active efforts to keep the family together, tell the child's tribe and parents about the case, and follow placement preferences that favor family and community. The tribe can join the case, and a parent or the tribe can ask to move it to tribal court. ICWA does not cover custody disputes between parents.
records.who: Families of children who are tribal members or eligible for membership. Each tribe sets its own membership rules.
records.start: If you think these rights are being ignored, NICWA says to contact a lawyer (with Indian and family law experience if you can find one), legal services, or the child's tribe right away.

records.name: UNITY: United National Indian Tribal Youth
records.what: A national network of Native youth councils that builds leadership through trainings and conferences. Councils can be tribal, village, urban, school or college groups.
records.who: American Indian, Alaska Native and Native Hawaiian youth, including descendants. Suggested ages 14 to 24.
records.start: Join through a youth council, or as an individual member for $50 a year. Call 480-718-9793 with questions.

records.name: We R Native: Ask Your Relatives
records.what: A site for Native youth where you can send a question to Auntie or Uncle and read answers to questions other young people have asked.
records.who: Native youth.
records.start: Open the Ask Your Relatives page and send your question. Giving your name is optional.

records.name: American Indian College Fund scholarships
records.what: Scholarships for Native students in certificate, undergraduate or graduate programs at tribal colleges and at accredited nonprofit colleges. One application a year covers all of its scholarships.
records.who: Students enrolled in a federally or state-recognized tribe, or descended from an enrolled member. High school seniors and students at non-tribal colleges need a 2.0 grade point average.
records.start: Applications open February 1. Apply by May 31 for priority; later applications are still accepted. For help, email scholarships@collegefund.org or call 800-987-3863.

records.name: Cobell Scholarship
records.what: Scholarships for undergraduate, graduate and vocational or trade students, to help with tuition, fees, books and living costs.
records.who: Enrolled members of a U.S. federally recognized tribe who study full time at an accredited nonprofit school.
records.start: Check the eligibility list and apply on the Cobell Scholarship site.

records.name: Tribal colleges and universities
records.what: The American Indian College Fund lists 34 accredited tribal colleges and universities, with a page for each. The Bureau of Indian Education runs two of them itself: Haskell Indian Nations University in Lawrence, Kansas, and Southwestern Indian Polytechnic Institute in Albuquerque, New Mexico.
records.who: Ask each college about admission.
records.start: Browse the list, then contact the college's admissions office.

more.label: Bureau of Indian Education: scholarships and internships

records.name: No place to stay tonight: emergency shelter
records.what: The federal housing department's direction for anyone who is homeless: dial 211 and press 6 for homeless services. Its Find Shelter tool lists local shelters, food pantries, health clinics and places to get clothing. USA.gov says 211 works in most areas of the United States and gives referrals for emergency housing.
records.who: Anyone.
records.start: Dial 211 and press 6. Say where you are and what you need tonight. If 211 does not connect, open the Find Shelter tool. Shelter space changes daily, so call before you travel.

records.name: National Call Center for Homeless Veterans
records.what: Free and confidential support, 24 hours a day, for veterans who are facing or experiencing homelessness.
records.who: Veterans, and people calling for a veteran.
records.start: Call 1-877-424-3838 and say where you are and what you need tonight.

records.name: Tribal housing programs
records.what: Federal housing money for Native communities goes to tribes through the Indian Housing Block Grant. Each tribe names a housing office, called a tribally designated housing entity, to run its programs, which can include housing services for families.
records.who: Each tribe's housing office sets who it serves.
records.start: Look up your tribe's housing office in HUD's National Tribal Housing Directory and ask what help is open and how to apply.

records.name: Section 184 Indian Home Loan Guarantee
records.what: A home loan backed by HUD for Native borrowers, with a 2.25% down payment. It can be used to buy, build, repair or refinance a home.
records.who: Currently enrolled members of federally recognized tribes.
records.start: Read HUD's page for borrowers, then contact a lender that takes part in Section 184.

records.name: BIA Housing Improvement Program
records.what: Grants to repair, renovate or replace a home for Native families who cannot get housing help from any other source.
records.who: Members of federally recognized tribes who live in an approved tribal service area, have income at or below 150% of the federal poverty guidelines, live in substandard housing or are homeless, and have no other resource.
records.start: Fill out BIA Form 6407 and mail or take it to your tribe's housing office (the Tribal Servicing Office).

records.name: Food Distribution Program on Indian Reservations (FDPIR)
records.what: USDA foods for households with low income living on reservations, and for American Indian households in approved areas near reservations and in Oklahoma. Many households use it instead of SNAP.
records.who: The tribal organizations and state agencies that run the program decide who qualifies.
records.start: Ask your tribe's food distribution program how to apply.

records.name: BIA financial assistance and social services
records.what: Help from the Bureau of Indian Affairs when other programs are not available: General Assistance for food, clothing, shelter and utilities; Emergency Assistance after a fire, flood or other disaster (up to $1,500 a household); Burial Assistance (up to $3,500); and payments toward the care of children and of adults who need daily help.
records.who: American Indians and Alaska Natives who cannot get TANF or have used it up. The application asks for proof of tribal membership, where you live, and your income.
records.start: Apply with a social worker at your tribe's social services office or BIA agency, using the Application for Financial Assistance and Social Services.

records.name: 211: local help with food, housing and bills
records.what: 211 connects you to local help with bills, food, housing, utilities, health costs, mental health and substance use. United Way's 211 site says every call is confidential.
records.who: Anyone.
records.start: Dial 211 and say what you need and your ZIP code. If 211 does not connect from your phone, use the website to find your local 211.

records.name: SNAP food benefits
records.what: SNAP helps people with low income buy food. You apply through your state or local SNAP office.
records.who: Anyone who meets the income rules.
records.start: Open the USDA page on how to apply. You apply through the SNAP office for your state.

records.name: Lifeline: a discount on phone or internet service
records.what: A federal discount of up to $9.25 a month on phone or internet service, or up to $34.25 a month on qualifying Tribal lands. You can qualify if someone in your household gets SSI, Medicaid, SNAP, federal public housing assistance or a Veterans Pension, or if household income is at or below 135% of the federal poverty guidelines.
records.who: Households that meet the rule above. One benefit per household.
records.start: Apply at LifelineSupport.org or by mail, then sign up with a phone or internet company that takes part.
records.phone_note: Lifeline Support Center, 9 a.m. to 9 p.m. Eastern, every day

records.name: Native job and training programs (WIOA Section 166)
records.what: The U.S. Department of Labor funds tribes and Native organizations across the country to give job search help, money for education and training, and support services to Native adults and youth.
records.who: American Indians, Alaska Natives and Native Hawaiians. Each grantee sets its own intake rules.
records.start: Find the grantee for your area and ask for its employment and training program. The state pages on this site name the grantees where we have them.
records.url_label: Division of Indian and Native American Programs

records.name: Tribal vocational rehabilitation projects
records.what: Tribal governments run vocational rehabilitation projects that help American Indians with disabilities prepare for and get jobs in a culturally relevant way. Services follow an individual plan for employment and may include native healing services. The federal Rehabilitation Services Administration lists 93 projects in 26 states.
records.who: American Indians and Alaska Natives with disabilities who live in a tribe's service area, on or near a reservation. Ask the project who it serves.
records.start: Ask your tribe's social services or health office whether it runs a tribal vocational rehabilitation project.

records.name: Finding legal help (Native American Rights Fund guide)
records.what: A guide from the National Indian Law Library to lawyers, legal aid programs and law school clinics that work on Indian law. The Native American Rights Fund is a nonprofit law firm that has represented tribal nations, organizations and individuals since 1970. It cannot take every request, and its lawyers do not handle criminal or family law cases.
records.who: Anyone looking for a lawyer for a tribal or federal Indian law problem.
records.start: Start with the guide. To ask the Native American Rights Fund itself for help, use its request form.

records.name: Free civil legal aid near you
records.what: The Legal Services Corporation funds nonprofit legal aid programs with offices in every state. They help people with low income with civil legal problems such as evictions, safety, income and family matters. Its programs serve households at or below 125% of the federal poverty guidelines.
records.who: People with low income. Each office decides which cases it can take.
records.start: Use the Get Legal Help search to find the office that serves you, then call or apply online. For a criminal case, ask the court for a court-appointed lawyer.

records.name: Contact any federally recognized Nation (BIA Tribal Leaders Directory)
records.what: The Bureau of Indian Affairs lists contact details for each federally recognized Nation, with a map. As of January 30, 2026 it counts 575 federally recognized tribes.
records.who: Anyone.
records.start: Use the Nations page on this site, which is built from this directory, or open the BIA directory itself.

records.name: Tracing Native ancestry and enrolling in a tribe (BIA guide)
records.what: The federal guide to working out which Nation your family comes from and applying to it. The BIA does not keep a list of enrolled members and does not do family research for people. Each tribe keeps its own records and sets its own rules.
records.who: Anyone with a Native ancestor.
records.start: Work out which tribe your ancestor belonged to, gather the birth and death certificates that link you to that person, then contact that tribe's enrollment office. Our Finding your Nation page walks through it.

more.label: How tribal enrollment works (Department of the Interior)

records.name: Indian boarding school records (National Indian Boarding School Digital Archive)
records.what: An archive of digitized boarding school records and student name lists, built by the National Native American Boarding School Healing Coalition so that survivors and descendants can find their families' records. The coalition has also mapped 523 Indian boarding schools.
records.who: Anyone. It was built for survivors and descendants.
records.start: Search the archive for the school or the family name.
records.url_label: National Indian Boarding School Digital Archive

records.name: Elder programs run by tribes (Older Americans Act, Title VI)
records.what: Tribal programs for elders: meals at a meal site or delivered at home, rides, help around the house, information and referral, and support for family caregivers, including grandparents raising grandchildren.
records.who: Each tribe decides the age at which someone counts as an elder.
records.start: Call your tribe's elder or senior program and ask about Title VI services.

records.name: Eldercare Locator
records.what: A free national call center from the U.S. Administration for Community Living. It connects older adults and their caregivers to the local Area Agency on Aging and other local help.
records.who: Older adults, people with disabilities and caregivers.
records.start: Call or text 1-800-677-1116 with a ZIP code or a city and state.

records.name: Veterans Crisis Line
records.what: Free, confidential crisis support for veterans and the people who care about them, 24 hours a day, 365 days a year.
records.who: Veterans, service members and their families.
records.start: Dial 988 and press 1, text 838255, or chat from the website.

records.name: No VA copays for Native veterans
records.what: Eligible American Indian and Alaska Native veterans do not pay VA copays for health care or urgent care. Copays still apply to domiciliary care, institutional respite care, institutional geriatric evaluation and nursing home care.
records.who: American Indian and Alaska Native veterans who send the VA their tribal documentation.
records.start: Send VA Form 10-334 with a copy of your official tribal documentation. For questions, call 1-800-698-2411.

records.name: Native American Direct Loan (VA home loan on trust land)
records.what: A VA loan to buy, build or improve a home on federal trust land, or to refinance one of these loans.
records.who: Native American veterans, and veterans married to a Native American. Your tribal government must have an agreement with the VA, and you need a VA home loan Certificate of Eligibility.
records.start: Check whether your tribe has an agreement with the VA, then call 888-349-7541 and ask for the NADL team.

more.label: Tribes that have an agreement with the VA
